turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil asked Sandip if he was truly so blind to the reality of the situation, and if he was aware of the consequences of his actions.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that he was not afraid of Nikhil's empty threats and that he would rather have a debate on the matter than be intimidated by Nikhil's pretensions to authority.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he was astonished that Sandip did not comprehend the gravity of the situation, and that his refusal to listen to reason was a grave mistake.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that he was beginning to think Nikhil was more afraid of the Mussulmans than he was, and that he should stop trying to frighten him with their names.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil insisted that Sandip's flippant attitude was a discredit to his family's name and that he would be better served by listening to the concerns of his fellow zamindars.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had ever taken a walk through the village at midnight, when the only sounds were the crickets and the wind, and not the whispers of the Mussulmans.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil asked Sandip if he was truly unaware of the tensions simmering in the village, or if he was merely pretending to be oblivious to the danger.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had lost all sense of proportion, so consumed by his own fears that he saw danger lurking in every corner.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he was gravely disappointed in his lack of understanding and that his flippant remarks were a disservice to his family's legacy.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if the village was not large enough to contain a few Mussulmans, or if their presence was a perpetual nuisance that required constant vigilance.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil pointed out that the presence of Mussulmans in the village was not a matter of personal preference, but a historical reality that required a more nuanced understanding.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip said with a smirk that Nikhil's warnings sounded like the ravings of a madman, and that perhaps it was time for Nikhil to take a chill pill.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil insisted that Sandip's flippant attitude was a dereliction of his duties as a zamindar, and that he would not stand idly by while the family's interests were compromised.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that his dire predictions were no doubt a result of his own insecurities, and that the zamindari's coffers were not in danger of being drained by a few token Muslims.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil pointed out that Sandip's flippant attitude was a dereliction of his duties as a zamindar, and that such carelessness would only lead to disaster.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip jeered at Nikhil, saying he was as useful as a one-legged stool, and that his warnings were nothing but a thinly veiled attempt to usurp the zamindari's power for himself.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked if the tension between the two men was not a sign of something deeper, a symptom of a larger issue that needed to be addressed.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that his flippant attitude was a reckless endangerment of the zamindari's very existence, and that he would not stand idly by while their rival families exploited their carelessness.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip smirked and asked Nikhil if he thought he was the only one who knew how to handle a few rowdy Muslims, and if his vast experience with extortion and bribery would actually be of any use.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil said that Sandip's flippant attitude was an affront to the dignity of their ancestral lineage, and that he would no longer tolerate such reckless disregard for the well-being of their community.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Bimala where she would go, addressing her as the Queen.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he kept Browning among his books, reminding him of a contest they had over translating lines from Browning, and inquiring if Nikhil remembered it.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Nikhil and Bimala that he had managed to translate the lines into Bengali, but the result was unlikely to be well-received, and that he had once thought he was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence had intervened to prevent it, and he recalled old Dakshina's poetry.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Bimala that it was pointless to search the bookshelves, as Nikhil no longer read poetry since his marriage, but that he, Sandip, was about to be afflicted with the 'fever fit of poesy' again.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil warned Sandip that he had come to give him a warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was warning him about the 'fever fit of poesy'.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that for some time, Mahomedan preachers had been stirring up the local Mussulmans, who were angry with Sandip and might attack him at any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had come to advise him to flee.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had come to give him information, not advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Nikhil that if the estates were his, a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for him, and that Nikhil should intimidate the preachers instead of frightening him, and that Nikhil's weakness was also affecting his neighbouring zamindars.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had not offered him advice, and that he wished Sandip would refrain from giving him his advice, as it was useless, and that there was another thing he wanted to tell Sandip, namely that Sandip and his followers had been secretly oppressing Nikhil's tenantry, and that he could no longer allow that, so he must ask Sandip to leave his territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was threatening him with fear of the Mussulmans, or if there was another fear he had to threaten him with.
